## Step 1

## Step 2

![Inversion recovery: Spin-lattice (T1) — step 2.](images/ch10/inversion-recovery-spin-lattice-t1-2.png){#fig-ch10-inversion-recovery-spin-lattice-t1-2}

## Step 3

![Inversion recovery: Spin-lattice (T1) — step 3.](images/ch10/inversion-recovery-spin-lattice-t1-3.png){#fig-ch10-inversion-recovery-spin-lattice-t1-3}

:::

In @fig-ch07-example-longitudinal-relaxation we asked what happens when the flip angle is 180 deg rather than 90 deg.  This is the answer, and it is the whole basis of the inversion recovery sequence.

A 90 deg pulse leaves the longitudinal component at zero, so it recovers from zero,

$$
M_z(t) = M_0\left(1 - e^{-t/T_1}\right)
$$

A 180 deg pulse *inverts* the net magnetization: it now points along $-z$, and it starts at $-M_0$ rather than at zero.  The recovery has the same exponential form, but it has twice as far to travel,

$$
M_z(t) = M_0\left(1 - 2e^{-t/T_1}\right)
$$

The factor of 2 is the only difference.  Because the magnetization has to climb all the way from $-M_0$ to $+M_0$, it passes through zero on the way, at $t = T_1 \ln 2 \approx 0.69\,T_1$.  That zero crossing is what makes the sequence useful: choosing the inversion time TI so that a particular tissue is passing through zero suppresses that tissue entirely, which is what FLAIR does with CSF.

There is one more wrinkle.  A 180 deg pulse produces no transverse magnetization, so it generates no signal by itself.  That is why the sequence needs the second, 90 deg pulse: it tips whatever longitudinal magnetization has recovered during TI into the transverse plane, where we can measure it.  The measured signal is therefore a snapshot of the T1 recovery at time TI.

## The signal magnitude formation when for 180 deg flip

![The signal magnitude formation when for 180 deg flip.](images/ch10/the-signal-magnitude-formation-when-for-180-deg-fl.png){#fig-ch10-the-signal-magnitude-formation-when-for-180-deg-fl}

The graphs above plot $M_z$ itself, with the values before the zero crossing shown as negative.  But we measure only the *magnitude* of the signal, which is always positive.  Taking the absolute value folds the negative part of the recovery upward, so the measured curve descends to zero at $t = T_1 \ln 2$ and then climbs again — the V shape on the right.  The position of that null is a direct read on T1, and tissues with different T1 values null at different inversion times.

The link on this page goes to a very nice web-site for quantitative MRI.

That site includes references to Joelle Barral and Nikola Stikov’s work in fitting these kinds of data.

Barral:  A robust methodology for in vivo T1 mapping

Stikov:  On the accuracy of T1 mapping: Searching for common ground

If you don’t want to just produce an image, but you want to know the T1, you can use this method by Joelle Barral at Stanford

Original method by Look Locker
